questions.question: Classify the three stages of a cup of rooibos tea — growing the bush in the Cederberg, processing and packing the leaves, and selling the boxes in a supermarket — into their sectors, and explain how one bad harvest can eventually reach the shop's shelf.
questions.expected_answer: Growing and cutting the rooibos bush is primary, because the raw material is harvested directly from nature. Fermenting, drying and packing the leaves into teabags is secondary, because a raw material is transformed into a manufactured product. Trucking, shelving and selling the boxes — along with the card payment and the advertising — is tertiary, because these are services. The sectors are interdependent stations on one line: a drought that withers the harvest leaves the processing plant short of leaves months later, output falls and prices rise, and the supermarket's shelf runs thin — trouble at the primary station rides the chain to the end.

questions.question: Describe South Africa's current economic structure with approximate shares, outline the historical shift that produced it, and explain what premature deindustrialisation means and why it matters here.
questions.expected_answer: Services dominate at roughly two thirds of GDP, led by finance and business services; the secondary sector supplies about one fifth, with manufacturing near 13%; and the primary sector is smallest, with mining around 6% and agriculture around 3% of GDP. Historically the economy moved from the mines-and-farms era through the factory decades of the mid-twentieth century to the services era from the 1980s onward — the ordered journey called structural transformation. Premature deindustrialisation is South Africa's defect in that journey: manufacturing peaked above 20% of GDP in the early 1990s and slid to about 13% before it had absorbed the workers leaving farms and mines. It matters because manufacturing is historically the great absorber of semi-skilled labour, which an economy with unemployment above 30% needs most, while many of the service jobs that replaced factory work demand qualifications excluded workers have not yet been able to earn.

questions.question: Using one concrete chain from the lesson, explain how unequal access to services becomes unequal economic opportunity.
questions.expected_answer: Services are the ticket at the gate of the economy, so a missing service raises a person's cost of participating, and it raises it most steeply for the poor. One full chain: a matric learner in a household without electricity cannot revise after sunset, enters the final examinations at a disadvantage, and carries that disadvantage into the job market. Other chains work identically: without affordable transport, a vacancy thirty kilometres away pays almost nothing once taxi fare is subtracted; without data, job adverts, price comparisons and cheap banking happen out of sight. In each case the gap in the pipe or cable becomes a gap in the person's chances, which is how infrastructure gaps copy inequality into the next generation.
